prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

How do we know Eve and Adam were happy, deprived, as they were, of a childhood? Eve never knew, unlike Adam, a world that was free of the chatter of others.’ How did she cope? And how could she choose, if she’d wanted, to live by herself? What did the man eat that made him hear voices, while Eve was inventing frustration? Where could she go for a break from the sound of Himself, in his skin suit, like Tarzan, assuring the bush that he’d just given birth to a woman? Did she smile at the fool, or remind him that he was asleep when she turned up and found him? Where could she go to be shot of his need for a mother? (A pity she woke him.) Life for them both was a training film shown in real time, on the zen of zoo-keeping. When the encyclopedia seller arrived, who could blame her for buying? No exit pollster asked how she felt when she left at the end of the movie.

prompts.L3:

- The text questions whether Adam and Eve could have been happy despite never experiencing childhood.
- Eve is portrayed as trapped with Adam’s constant chatter and unable to choose solitude or escape his presence.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: How, Eve, Adam

outputs.L1: How do we know that Eve and Adam were happy, deprived as they were of a childhood? Unlike Adam, Eve had never known a world free from the chatter of others. How did she cope? And how could she have chosen, had she wanted, to live by herself? What did the man eat that made him hear voices while Eve was inventing frustration? Where could she go to escape the sound of Himself, in his skin suit like Tarzan, assuring the bush that he had just given birth to a woman? Did she smile at the fool, or remind him that he had been asleep when she turned up and found him? Where could she go to be rid of his need for a mother? (A pity she woke him.) For them both, life was a training film, shown in real time, on the Zen of zookeeping. When the encyclopedia seller arrived, who could blame her for buying? No exit pollster asked how she felt when she left at the end of the movie.
outputs.L2: Can we really be sure that Adam and Eve were content when neither had ever been a child? Adam had once experienced a place untouched by anyone else’s talk, but Eve entered existence with another voice already filling it. How did she endure that, and, had solitude appealed to her, what opportunity did she have to pursue it? What had Adam consumed that caused him to hear things while Eve was discovering exasperation? Where might she escape the noise of Him—dressed only in his own hide, Tarzan-like, announcing to the vegetation that he had produced a woman? Did she humor the idiot with a smile, or point out that he had been unconscious when she appeared and came upon him? How could she free herself from his longing to be mothered? It was unfortunate that she roused him. Their shared existence resembled an instructional movie unfolding live, a lesson in the meditative art of managing a zoo. So when the peddler of encyclopedic knowledge showed up, who could fault her for making a purchase? And when the film finished and she departed, no one conducting an exit survey was there to ask for her reaction.
outputs.L3:
The text questions the traditional image of Adam and Eve as perfectly happy inhabitants of Eden. It asks whether they could truly have been content when neither of them had experienced childhood—a formative period associated with play, discovery, care, and gradual independence. Without such a past, their apparent innocence may seem less like bliss and more like emotional incompleteness.

Eve’s situation is portrayed as especially restrictive. She is trapped in Adam’s constant company and subjected to his endless chatter, with no real opportunity to seek solitude or escape his presence. Even Adam’s claim that he created Eve is treated mockingly: since he was asleep when she appeared, his insistence on taking credit seems both irrational and self-important.

Their relationship is further complicated by Adam’s apparent need for a mother rather than an equal companion. Eve is therefore burdened with caring for and managing him, turning life in paradise into an absurd lesson in domestic captivity. Eden becomes not a place of perfect freedom, but an environment in which Eve has little choice, privacy, or independence.

Against this background, her encounter with the so-called “encyclopedia seller” can be understood as an attempt to gain the knowledge denied to her. Her eventual departure is likewise framed not simply as disobedience, but as a reasonable effort to escape confinement and pursue intellectual and personal freedom. From this perspective, Eve’s actions represent a desire to become fully conscious and autonomous rather than a straightforward fall from innocence.
outputs.L4:
The passage reimagines the biblical story of Adam and Eve through a series of satirical rhetorical questions that invite readers to reconsider Eve’s experience in Eden. Rather than depicting paradise as a place of perfect happiness, it asks what life there would actually have been like for the first woman. Eve had no childhood, no mother or female companions, and no opportunity to grow into adulthood gradually. She entered the world already expected to fulfill a predetermined role as Adam’s partner. By emphasizing these absences, the passage exposes how little freedom or personal identity the traditional story grants her.

The questions also draw attention to Eve’s lack of privacy and autonomy. Eden may have offered beauty and abundance, but it provided no escape from Adam’s presence, expectations, or demands. Eve could not retreat into a private space, seek advice from others, or imagine a life independent of him. The satire therefore undermines the conventional image of Eden as an unquestionable paradise. From Eve’s perspective, such perfection may have felt restrictive, monotonous, and even oppressive.

Against this background, Eve’s decision to eat the forbidden fruit becomes more understandable. Her choice is not presented simply as an act of disobedience, vanity, or moral weakness. Instead, it represents curiosity, a desire for knowledge, and an attempt to gain control over her own existence. Leaving Eden, despite the pain and uncertainty that follow, offers the possibility of experience, change, and self-determination. The world outside paradise may be difficult, but it also allows Eve to become more than the passive companion she was created to be.

By presenting the story in this way, the passage challenges the traditional tendency to blame Eve for humanity’s fall. Its humor and rhetorical questions expose the assumptions underlying that judgment, especially the expectation that women should accept imposed roles without resistance. Eve’s departure from Eden can therefore be understood not merely as a fall from innocence, but as a bid for freedom, knowledge, and an identity of her own.
outputs.L5:
**How Eve Asked Adam**

“How do you know the world is ours?” Eve asked Adam as dawn spread gold across the garden.

Adam looked at the rivers, the trees, and the animals moving through the grass. “Perhaps it isn’t ours,” he replied. “Perhaps we are only here to care for it.”

Eve smiled and picked up a fallen seed. “Then we should begin by planting this.”

Together, Eve and Adam pressed the seed into the earth—not as rulers of the garden, but as its first guardians.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a witty feminist prose poem retelling Adam and Eve’s life in Eden from Eve’s perspective, questioning whether either of them was truly happy.
counterfactuals.output:
At first, there was no word for lonely.

There was garden, certainly—figs splitting with sweetness, rivers showing off, lilies with their mouths full of light. There was Adam, too, naming everything as if the world were a conference and he had the only clipboard.

“Lion,” he said.

The lion yawned.

“Rose.”

The rose, already perfectly aware of herself, declined to comment.

Then I arrived, allegedly from his rib, which is a flattering way to say history needed me to begin as a footnote. Adam woke, saw me, and looked relieved—as though God had finally delivered the second half of his conversation.

Was I happy? Imagine being born into perfection and immediately assigned a husband.

He was kind. Let that be said. Kind in the untested way of someone who has never had to choose between kindness and power. He showed me the paths, though my feet knew walking. He introduced me to the moon, though she and I had already exchanged a glance.

At night, we lay beneath stars so numerous they seemed less like decoration than evidence. Adam slept deeply. Innocence does. I listened to the dark breathing beyond the hedges and wondered why paradise needed boundaries.

God visited in the evenings. His voice made the leaves stand still. He asked Adam questions and Adam answered for both of us. This, I learned, was called harmony.

There was one tree we must not touch. Naturally, it stood in the center, where every path became an arrow pointing toward it. Divine interior design has never been subtle.

Adam said, “We have everything else.”

But everything else is a phrase often used by those who are not curious.

The serpent did not seduce me. He did something far more dangerous: he asked what I thought.

Perhaps he lied. Perhaps God did. Perhaps every birth begins with competing stories and a woman blamed for choosing one. I held the fruit. Its skin was taut and bright, a small red world refusing to apologize for its appetite.

I bit.

The taste was not evil. It was knowledge: sharp, seeded, difficult to swallow. Suddenly I saw Adam—not Man, not companion, but a person, frightened and beautiful and separate from me. I saw myself seeing him. I saw that nakedness was not the body but the moment you realize another person can judge it.

Adam ate because I offered. Or because he wanted to. History has always preferred the first version; it keeps his hunger innocent.

Were we happy before? Adam says yes, sometimes. He remembers endless afternoons, the animals coming when called, the absence of sweat. I remember the silence after I asked why.

Were we happy after? We had pain, certainly. Weather. Laundry. Sons who turned sorrow into inheritance. We learned that love is not the same as agreement, that labor means both childbirth and bread, that God’s voice grows fainter as your own grows louder.

Outside Eden, Adam stopped naming things and began asking me what I called them.

Not always. But sometimes.

We grew old. He missed the garden like a country that had never required him to become himself. I missed it like a room in which I had been safe but not free. At dusk, we would sit together, our hands rough, our knees aching, watching the world continue without permission.

“Were you happy there?” he asked me once.

I looked at him—my first mistake, my first witness, my fellow exile.

“I don’t know,” I said. “I wasn’t awake.”

And because he had eaten too, because knowledge is a door that locks behind you, he nodded.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Reimagine Genesis as a darkly comic contemporary monologue in which Eve is irritated by Adam’s chatter, dependence, and claim to have created her.
counterfactuals.output:
The first thing Adam ever said to me was, “Technically, you came from me.”

Imagine waking up to that.

No hello. No “How are you feeling?” No “Sorry about the rib situation.” Just a naked man crouching over me, pointing at his chest like he’d personally completed a difficult flat-pack wardrobe.

“Bone of my bone,” he said.

I said, “Could you stand somewhere else?”

There was an entire garden. Acres of somewhere else. But Adam had already developed the habit of hovering. He followed me past the fig trees, through the lilies, around the river, narrating everything he’d named.

“Those are cattle.”

“I can see them.”

“That’s a hawk.”

“It’s eating a mouse.”

“Yes,” he said proudly, as though he’d designed the system.

He never stopped talking. He’d had nobody to talk to before I arrived, and apparently the silence had fermented inside him. Now it came pouring out: observations, theories, complaints about humidity. He explained trees to me. He explained thirst while I was drinking. He explained my own elbow.

At night he’d say, “Do you think the stars are holes?”

“In what?”

He had no answer, but that didn’t slow him down.

And the dependence. God made me as a “helper,” which is a lovely word if you enjoy doing all the work while someone else takes credit for inventing teamwork.

Adam couldn’t find anything.

“Eve, where’s the good rock?”

“Eve, have you seen my fig leaf?”

“Eve, which berries make your tongue swell?”

“The blue ones.”

“They’re all blue at night.”

“Then stop eating in the dark.”

Sometimes I wondered how he’d survived before me. Then I remembered: he hadn’t had to. Nothing had teeth yet, and food grew at face level.

Still, he regarded himself as the senior partner.

“You were made from my rib,” he reminded me whenever I disagreed with him.

“Yes, Adam. You’ve mentioned it.”

“It means there’s a connection.”

“It means God used locally available materials.”

He didn’t like that.

Then there was the tree.

You know the one. Everyone does. Nobody remembers the thousands of other trees—almond, olive, pomegranate, pear. One tree gets a warning label and suddenly history is merchandise.

God had said not to eat from it. Adam repeated this constantly, usually while standing under it.

“We mustn’t,” he’d say, staring up at the fruit.

“I’m not.”

“It would be bad.”

“I understand.”

“Possibly fatal.”

“Then move away from the tree.”

He never did.

The serpent, when it finally spoke, was almost a relief. At least it asked questions. At least it didn’t begin with “Technically.”

“Did God really say you must not eat from any tree?” it asked.

“No,” I said. “Just this one.”

“Curious.”

“Very.”

“Knowledge,” said the serpent, “is wasted on people who don’t want it.”

We both looked at Adam. He was trying to name an insect that had already bitten him three times.

I took the fruit.

Not because I was hungry. Not because I was deceived. Not even because I wanted to be like God.

I wanted five minutes in which Adam did not know more than I did.

I bit.

The world sharpened.

I saw death. Work. Childbirth. War. Property law. Advertising. I saw Adam in every century, leaning over a woman’s desk and saying, “What you need to understand is—”

Then Adam appeared beside me.

“What are you eating?”

“Consequences.”

“Can I have some?”

Of course he could. He always wanted what I had. My shade, my attention, my half of the sleeping moss. I handed him the fruit.

He ate without asking a single follow-up question.

That part tends to get lost.

A moment later he looked down and discovered nudity.

“We’re naked!”

“We’ve been naked all week.”

“But now I know.”

“Yes,” I said. “That’s rather the issue.”

When God came walking through the garden, Adam hid behind me.

Then God asked what happened.

Adam stepped out and said, “The woman you gave me—”

There it was. The first passive voice. The first blame shifted neatly across a room.

I looked at him: this man who claimed he had made me, yet couldn’t be responsible for anything I did. My creator when he wanted authority; my victim when he wanted mercy.

God pronounced the punishments. Pain, toil, thorns, mortality. Adam wept. I made a list.

By sunset we were outside the gates.

Adam carried nothing. I had packed fruit, water, seeds, flint, and two sturdy leaves.

He gazed into the wilderness.

“What do we do now?” he asked.

Behind us, Eden burned gold beneath the angel’s sword. Ahead: weather, wolves, history.

I handed him the smaller bag.

“First,” I said, “you stop telling people you made me.”

He opened his mouth.

“And second?”

I walked on.

Behind me, after only a moment, came the sound of him following.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a short literary passage about Eve’s loneliness in the Garden of Eden, using rhetorical questions, anachronisms, and satirical references to Tarzan, encyclopedia sellers, movies, and exit polls.
counterfactuals.output:
Eve wandered beneath trees that had never heard an axe and wondered, *Is perfection still paradise when no one asks how your day was?* Adam was off naming beetles, a task he pursued with the solemnity of an encyclopedia salesman certain the household lacked Volume B.

She tried speaking to the serpent, but he had the oily confidence of a studio executive pitching *Tarzan: The Original Man*. “You’ll love it,” he hissed. “Very primal. Strong demographics.”

Was she lonely, or merely ahead of her time? There were no movies to escape into, no cafés in which to brood, not even an exit poll to tell her whether humanity approved of her choices. By sunset, the Garden glowed like a lavish set after the actors had gone home.

“Paradise,” Eve said to the silence. “According to whom?”
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an irreverent, intellectually playful prose poem that portrays Eden as a zoo and the serpent as a persuasive salesperson offering Eve knowledge.
counterfactuals.output:
**Eden, Inc.**

Eden was less a paradise than a zoo with excellent landscaping.  
No cages, technically—just tasteful hedges, invisible policies,  
and a management sign reading:

**PLEASE DO NOT FEED THE CONSCIOUSNESS.**

Adam named the animals because somebody had to do the paperwork.  
“Giraffe,” he said, with the confidence of a man inventing necks.  
“Beetle.”  
“Other beetle.”  
“Extremely similar beetle.”

Eve, meanwhile, had begun to suspect the cosmos was withholding  
the footnotes.

Then the serpent arrived, sleek as a loophole,  
wearing no tie but somehow adjusting one.

“Madam,” he hissed, “how would you like to upgrade  
from Innocence Basic to Knowledge Premium?  
For one small bite, you receive moral complexity,  
seasonal shame, agriculture, metaphysics,  
and the thrilling awareness that everything dies.”

Eve examined the fruit.  
It shone with the vulgar confidence of a luxury product.

“Is there a warranty?”

“Better,” said the serpent. “There are consequences.”

Nearby, God moved mysteriously through the shrubbery,  
which is what management does when customers ask questions.

The animals watched. The lion had no opinion.  
The owl pretended this was old news.  
A pair of rabbits began multiplying in protest.

Eve bit.

At once the zoo acquired bars.  
Not around the beasts—around the mind.  
Every leaf became a thesis. Every body, a rumor.  
Adam discovered nudity and immediately blamed the dress code.

The serpent smiled, already slithering toward the next account.

“Congratulations,” he called.  
“You now qualify for doubt, art, dentistry,  
and the long, glittering disaster of civilization.”

And outside the gift shop,  
the world opened its enormous mouth.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a feminist revision of the Adam and Eve story in a sharp, surreal style, exploring Eve’s lack of privacy, Adam’s need for mothering, and her decision to leave paradise.
counterfactuals.output:
At first there were no doors.

God had invented light, darkness, oceans, teeth, milk, thunder, figs, and the small blue flame that lives inside certain beetles—but not doors. Privacy had not occurred to Him.

Eve discovered this omission immediately.

Wherever she went, the garden watched. Orchids opened their wet mouths. Sparrows reported from the branches. God’s eye hung in the sky like a gold coin that could not be spent. Even sleep had no walls. Her dreams were public property.

Adam did not mind.

“Why would anyone need to be alone?” he asked, resting his head in her lap.

He had been born a grown man and considered this a tragedy everyone else should manage. He wanted Eve to name the fruits he had forgotten, untangle burrs from his hair, praise his ideas, listen to his fears, and wake before him so the morning would feel prepared.

When he was hungry, he looked astonished.

When he was tired, he became philosophical.

When he was frightened, he called it love and reached for her.

“You’re better at these things,” he said, though no one had taught her either.

Eve began building a room inside herself.

She furnished it with silence. She hung curtains over her eyes. Behind them she kept thoughts with their shoes off: What if kindness is not the same as service? What if love is not a job assigned to the nearest woman? What if paradise is merely a cage with excellent weather?

The serpent found her there.

It did not slither down a tree. It arrived through a crack in the afternoon, wearing the green skin of a question.

“Do you want knowledge?” it asked.

“I want a lock,” Eve said.

The serpent smiled. Its mouth opened sideways.

“Same thing.”

The tree stood in the center of the garden like a red alarm. Its fruit pulsed faintly, as if each apple contained a heart considering escape.

God had said not to touch it. He had not explained why. Rules, Eve noticed, were often called sacred when explanation would make them look small.

She plucked the fruit.

At once, every bird went silent. The sky leaned closer.

She bit.

Knowledge did not enter her like sunlight. It entered like a knife discovering it had always been a key.

She saw the garden’s machinery: the vines trained to conceal the walls, the lions drugged with innocence, the angels posted like guards at a nursery. She saw Adam’s helplessness polished into authority. She saw her own care transformed, by repetition, into destiny.

She saw God naming obedience peace.

Adam came running.

“What have you done?” he cried.

He looked first at the fruit, then at Eve, then around for someone to tell him what to feel.

“Eat,” she said, handing it to him.

He did, because even his rebellion needed serving.

Then they saw they were naked.

Adam covered himself and blamed the temperature.

Eve covered herself because, for the first time, her body felt like a country with borders.

God arrived in a storm of disappointed furniture. Trees bent into pews. Stones arranged themselves as witnesses.

“Where are you?” He called.

Eve almost laughed. After all that watching, He wanted her to confess her location.

“I am here,” Adam said quickly, stepping from behind a bush. “The woman—”

Of course, Eve thought.

He pointed at her with the solemn relief of a child who has found his mother.

God spoke of punishment: blood, labor, pain, hunger, thorns. Adam trembled. Eve listened carefully.

Outside the garden, there would be death.

But there would also be distance.

There would be caves, doors, rooms, roads vanishing over hills. There would be nights without a divine eye burning overhead. There would be work that belonged to the person doing it. There would be children, perhaps, but she would not confuse creating life with owing everyone hers.

“Please,” Adam whispered, “tell Him you’re sorry.”

Eve looked at the gates. Beyond them, the world was unfinished and roaring. Snow sharpened the mountains. Wolves moved through the dark with no shame. The moon floated alone, magnificent in her privacy.

An angel raised a flaming sword.

To Adam, it looked like exile.

To Eve, it looked like a door.

She stepped toward it.

Adam caught her wrist. “What will happen to me?”

The old answer rose automatically: I’ll take care of you.

She swallowed it whole.

“You’ll learn,” she said.

Then she walked out of paradise, carrying no luggage but her body, which was finally her own.

Behind her, Adam called her name as though it meant come back.

Ahead, the wilderness called nothing.

It did not know her.

It did not need her.

It made room.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
